# Layered Docs

Use this skill when a document needs to work for more than one type of reader —
someone who just wants the overview, someone who needs the technical detail, and
someone who needs to know how to use it.

This skill governs audience layering: who needs which part of the document and
where that part should live. For technical completeness, use
`picture-first-docs`. For concrete rewrites, use `rewrite-not-review`.

## Core Rule

Write for the busiest reader first.

Give them enough to understand what this is and why it matters — without
needing to read the whole thing. Then let the detail be there for whoever
wants it, organized so it's easy to find.

The goal isn't a short document. It's a document where every reader finds what
they need quickly, and nobody has to slog through stuff that isn't for them.

## Four Audience Layers

Project docs often serve four kinds of readers:

| Layer | Reader | What they need |
|---|---|---|
| Overview | Project manager, stakeholder | Why does this exist? What changes? Is it on track? |
| Detail | Engineer, implementer, reviewer | How does it work? What are the exact rules? What are the edge cases? |
| Usage | User, operator | How do I use this? What do I do when something goes wrong? |
| Agent | AI implementer | What exactly do I do? What are the exact files, commands, and scope? |

Not every document needs all four layers. But when you're writing, ask: who is
going to read this, and what do they need to leave with?

Structure the document so each reader can stop when they have enough.

## Document Shape

Always go big picture first, then zoom in.

This default shape works best for README files, handbook pages, feature
overviews, and mixed-audience specs. Architecture docs and work-package handoffs
may need a tighter technical shape; use `picture-first-docs` for completeness
and the Agent layer below for exact implementation handoffs.

Default order:

1. **TL;DR** — 2–4 bullets. What is this, why does it exist, what's the main change.
2. **Why this exists** — One short paragraph. The problem it solves, or the opportunity it takes.
3. **What it does** — What changed or what the feature does. Use before/after pairs for visible changes.
4. **How to use it** — Step-by-step for the user. Plain language. What they type, click, or see.
5. **How it works** — The technical detail. Architecture, data shapes, edge cases. Link to deeper docs instead of repeating.
6. **Limitations and edge cases** — What it doesn't do, known constraints, fallback behavior.
7. **Where to read more** — Links to architecture docs, specs, command references.

Skip sections that don't apply. Never pad.

## Layer Boundaries

Use plain language in Overview and Usage layers, even when the technical term is
familiar to the team. In Detail and Agent layers, project terms are fine after
they are defined once.

If a section is getting long, decide whether it belongs in another layer or
another document. Do not solve a confusing overview by adding more sections.

For each section, choose one:

- keep here because every reader needs it
- move lower because only implementers need it
- move to another file because it is reference material
- delete because it repeats a fact already explained better elsewhere

## Agent-Facing Sections

Use this when the reader is an AI implementer, reviewer, or handoff agent.
Friendly prose still matters, but precision matters more.

Agent-facing sections should include:

- exact files and folders to read
- exact files and folders that may be changed
- protected files or folders that must not be changed
- literal commands to run, including validation commands
- expected outputs, exit behavior, or pass/fail signals
- decisions already made, plus decisions intentionally deferred
- stop conditions that require asking for scope or clarification

Avoid phrases that require inference, such as "clean this up," "make it
reasonable," or "handle edge cases." Name the edge cases.

## Skim Test

Before finishing, read only:

- The TL;DR
- The headings
- The first sentence of each section

If a project manager can't tell what this is and why it matters from just
those — revise before adding more detail.

## Must Not

- Open with context before the point. Lead with what matters.
- Write a usage section that assumes the reader already knows the internals.
- Write formally. This isn't a legal document.
- Use jargon as a shortcut for clarity.
- Leave the usage layer out of a user-facing spec.
- Skip the TL;DR on any document longer than one screen.
- Give an agent-facing handoff that requires guessing scope, files, commands, or
  pass/fail criteria.
